sections.title: Prologue
sections.html:
Prologue

June 9. 3:12 a.m.

The headlights have been behind her since the gatehouse.

Lucy Brandt grips the wheel of her little blue Honda and takes the first switchback too fast, the tires squealing on wet asphalt. Fog pours across the road in slow white rivers. On her left, the mountain. On her right, a guardrail, and beyond it, nothing at all. Six hundred feet of nothing, all the way down to the valley floor.

The headlights take the curve behind her. High beams. Close.

She fumbles her phone out of the cup holder with one hand and thumbs the only name she can think of. The one she hasn't called in two years.

It rings. And rings.

"Pick up," Lucy whispers. "Please. Please pick up."

The voicemail greeting starts, a voice so familiar it makes her throat close. You've reached W. Leave a message.

"It's me." Her voice cracks. "I know you're still mad. I know. But I need you to listen. There's a woman up here who's supposed to be dead, and I've seen her, and they know I've seen her, and if anything happens to me—"

The headlights fill her mirror. White. Blinding.

The impact comes from behind, a hard metal kiss against her bumper, and the Honda slews sideways toward the guardrail, and Lucy drops the phone and grabs the wheel with both hands and screams.

The phone, on the floor mat, is still recording.

sections.title: Chapter 1
sections.html:
Chapter 1

Rule #1: Clock in at ten. Clock out at six. Never stay late.

Hollis Ridge sits at the top of the mountain like a crown somebody forgot to take off.

It was built in 1904 by a tobacco baron who wanted to look down on everyone, and it still does. Three stories of gray stone, a slate roof, turrets at either end. A wide porch with white rocking chairs that nobody rocks in. Around it, the Blue Ridge folds away in every direction, ridge after ridge, each one bluer and fainter than the last, until they dissolve into the sky.

There's one road up. Eleven switchbacks. I counted them on the way.

"Most people get carsick," Dr. Evelyn Hart says, leading me through the front hall. "You look fine."

"I have a strong stomach."

"Good. You'll need it." She smiles. "That's a joke. Mostly."

Dr. Hart is in her late fifties, silver-haired and straight-backed, in a navy dress and pearls, like she's about to chair a board meeting. She walks fast. Her heels click on the marble floor. Everything about Hollis Ridge is marble or mahogany or brass, polished until it glows. There's a chandelier in the front hall the size of my car. There's a grand piano nobody plays. The air smells like lemon oil and lilies and, very faintly, underneath, the sharp chemical ghost of a hospital.

"We have eleven residents," she says. "All private pay. All from families who can afford the very best, and who expect it. Our day staff is excellent. Our night staff is small. You'll work alongside Tomas, who has been with us for twenty years, and our security officer, Gus, is in the gatehouse. Your job is simple. Keep them safe. Keep them comfortable. Keep them asleep."

"Understood."

She stops at a door marked OFFICE and turns to look at me. Her eyes are a very pale gray.

"Your résumé is impressive, Ms. Calder. Eight years in the ICU at Charlotte Memorial. You're overqualified for this position by a mile." She tilts her head. "So why are you here?"

I've practiced this answer in the mirror. "I burned out. Twelve-hour shifts, codes every night, people dying on me. I needed somewhere quiet."

"Well." Dr. Hart opens the office door. "It's very quiet here."

* * *

The office is small and old-fashioned, with a rolltop desk and a green-shaded lamp. On the wall, there's a whiteboard with residents' names and room numbers. On the desk, a baby monitor, the old-fashioned kind with a little row of red lights. It hisses faintly with static.

Dr. Hart takes a laminated card from a drawer and hands it to me.

"The night rules," she says. "Every night attendant gets a copy. There's one posted at the nurses' station, too."

I read it.

HOLLIS RIDGE: NIGHT SHIFT RULES

1. Clock in at ten. Clock out at six. Never stay late.

2. Rounds every hour, on the hour. Every door. Every resident.

3. No resident leaves their room after midnight. If you find one in the hall, walk them back. Do not ask where they were going.

4. Never answer the call button in Room 12.

5. The east elevator is out of service. Do not get in, even if it arrives.

6. If Mrs. Vale asks what year it is, tell her 1987.

7. The medication carts lock at two. Only Dr. Hart holds the key.

8. There are no night visitors. If you see one, you didn't.

9. Whatever you hear on the office monitor is not your concern.

I read it twice. My face doesn't move. I'm good at that. Eight years of telling families we're doing everything we can will do that to you.

"Room 12," I say.

"Has been empty for three years. The call system is old. Sometimes it glitches." Dr. Hart's voice is perfectly pleasant. "We've had electricians up. They can't find the fault. It's easier to ignore it."

"And the elevator?"

"Also old. Also glitchy." She smiles again. "This is a hundred-and-twenty-year-old house, Ms. Calder. It has its moods."

"And number eight? No night visitors?"

"Some of our residents have dementia. They see things. Husbands who died decades ago. Children who are grown and gone. If a resident tells you they had a visitor, you nod and you walk them back to bed." She takes the card from my hand, and for a second her fingers rest on mine. They're very cold. "You'd be amazed how much trouble comes from people who see things they shouldn't."

"I'm sure."

"The last night attendant," Dr. Hart says, and then pauses, like she's deciding whether to go on. "Lucy. She had a car accident on the way home from her shift, back in June. That road can be treacherous in the fog. It was a terrible loss."

"I'm sorry to hear that."

"She was a sweet girl. A little troubled, I think." Dr. Hart hands the card back to me. "Clock out at six, Ms. Calder. Drive slowly. And never stay late."

My hand is steady when I take the card. I make sure of it.

sections.title: Chapter 2
sections.html:
Chapter 2

Rule #2: Rounds every hour, on the hour. Every door. Every resident.

My first shift starts at 10:00 p.m. on a Tuesday in October. When I pull into the staff lot, there's only one other vehicle there, an old pickup parked under the single floodlight, beaded with fog.

Tomas meets me at the nurses' station. He's somewhere in his sixties, short and thick-chested, with a gray braid down his back and forearms like tree roots. He wears navy scrubs and orthopedic shoes, and he moves through the dark halls of Hollis Ridge like he's part of the building.

"You're the new one," he says. It isn't a question.

"Wren."

He considers that. "Like the bird."

"Like the bird."

"Hm." He hands me a flashlight, a ring of keys, and a clipboard. "Rounds every hour. You knock soft. You open the door. You look. Breathing, not breathing. Wet, not wet. On the floor, not on the floor. You write it down. You close the door."

"I've done rounds before."

"Not here." He starts walking. "Here is different."

* * *

The residents live on the second floor, in two long wings that stretch east and west from a central staircase. The nurses' station sits at the top of the stairs, in the middle, like a heart. Tomas walks me down the west wing first.

Room 1: Mr. Harold Pruitt, ninety-one, retired federal judge. Room 2: Mrs. Georgia Lynde, eighty-eight. Room 3: Mr. Samuel Okafor, eighty-four, a former cardiologist, who snores so loudly the door rattles. And on down the hall. Eleven residents in eleven rooms. Eleven sleeping faces in the beam of my flashlight, old and soft and vulnerable, like children.

At the far end of the west wing, the hall ends in a door.

It's the same as the others: dark wood, brass knob, brass number. 12. But there's no name card in the little holder beside it. And the brass knob is dull with dust.

Above the door, set into the wall, there's a small round light. Unlit. The call light.

"Room 12," Tomas says.

"Empty for three years," I say. "Dr. Hart told me."

Tomas looks at me for a long moment. His eyes are dark and hard to read.

"Rule four," he says, and turns around, and walks back the way we came.

* * *

The east wing is the mirror of the west, except at the end of the hall, there's no Room 12. There's an elevator. An old one, with a brass gate and a pair of scratched steel doors behind it. Taped across the doors, a sign, the paper yellowed: OUT OF SERVICE.

Above the doors is a brass half-moon dial with an arrow that points to the floor numbers. B, 1, 2, 3.

And one more. Past the 3, at the very end of the arc, where the arrow can barely reach. A single letter.

A.

"What's A?" I ask.

"Attic." Tomas doesn't look at the elevator. "Nobody goes up there."

"Then why does the elevator go there?"

"It doesn't." He turns and walks away. "It's out of service."

* * *

The night goes slow. That's what nights are. I've worked them for eight years, and I know their rhythm: the long quiet stretches, the small sounds, the way time goes thick and syrupy around three in the morning, when the body wants to sleep and the mind won't let it.

I do my rounds. Eleven, midnight, one, two. Everyone breathing. Nobody wet. Nobody on the floor.

At two o'clock, the medication carts lock with a small electronic click, all at once, both of them.

At 3:12, the call light above Room 12 comes on.

I'm at the nurses' station, filling in my clipboard. I hear it before I see it: a soft chime from the console on the desk, and a little red light blinking on the panel beside a label that reads 12. I look up, down the long dark hall of the west wing, and at the far end, above the dusty door, the round light is glowing. Red.

It's 3:12.

I look at the clock on the wall to be sure. Then I look at the clock on my phone. 3:12. 3:12. My hands have gone cold.

The chime sounds again.

"Rule four."

Tomas is standing behind me. I didn't hear him come. He reaches past me and presses a button on the console, and the chime stops. The light above Room 12 stays on for a few more seconds. Then it goes out.

"It does that," Tomas says. "Every night. Around three."

"Every night?"

"Every night for three years." He sits down in the other chair and folds his thick hands on his stomach and closes his eyes. "You get used to it."

I look down the hall at the dark door.

I don't think I will.

sections.title: Chapter 3
sections.html:
Chapter 3

Rule #3: No resident leaves their room after midnight. If you find one in the hall, walk them back. Do not ask where they were going.

On my third night, I find Mrs. Vale in the hallway at 1:40 in the morning.

She's standing in the middle of the east wing in a pink quilted bathrobe and one slipper, facing the out-of-service elevator. She's tiny, maybe ninety pounds, with a cloud of white hair and eyes so blue they look painted. She's staring at the brass dial above the doors.

"Mrs. Vale?" I say softly. "It's Wren. The night nurse. Let's get you back to bed."

She doesn't turn around. "It went up."

"What did?"

"The elevator. It went up. It always goes up, and then it comes down." She finally turns to me, and her face is bright and curious, like a child's. "Is it 1987?"

I think of the laminated card in my pocket. If Mrs. Vale asks what year it is, tell her 1987.

"Yes," I say. "It's 1987."

Her whole face relaxes. "Oh, good. Then Marian's still here. I thought I'd missed her."

"Marian?"

"She's upstairs. She rings for me." Mrs. Vale pats my arm. "We used to sneak cigarettes on the back stairs, when the nurses weren't looking. She was very naughty. Everybody thought she was so proper. She wasn't."

Do not ask where they were going.

"Mrs. Vale," I say, very gently, "who's Marian?"

She blinks at me. "Marian. Marian Hart. It's her house, dear. Didn't they tell you?"

* * *

I walk her back to Room 9 and tuck her in. She's asleep before I reach the door.

At the nurses' station, I pull up the resident records on the ancient desktop computer. There's no Marian Hart in the current residents. I try the archive. It's password-protected.

Hart. Like Dr. Evelyn Hart.

"Her mother," says a voice behind me, and I nearly jump out of my skin.

It's Mr. Pruitt. Room 1. Ninety-one years old, bald as an egg, with enormous ears and bushy white eyebrows, standing in the doorway of his room in a plaid bathrobe, leaning on a cane with a silver handle.

"Mr. Pruitt, you're supposed to be in bed."

"I'm ninety-one. I haven't slept since the Carter administration." He waves a hand at the computer. "You're looking for Marian Hart. Evelyn's mother. She used to live in this house, you know. Grew up here. Evelyn turned it into this"—he gestures at the hall—"after the family money ran thin. And when Marian's mind started going, Evelyn moved her into Room 12."

"Room 12," I repeat.

"Died there. Three years ago this December." He squints at me. "You play chess?"

"What? I, a little."

"Good. Nobody here plays chess. Okafor cheats and Georgia eats the pieces." He turns back toward his room. "Come on. It's not like either of us is going to sleep."

* * *

Mr. Pruitt has a chessboard set up by his window, an old wooden one with pieces worn smooth by decades of hands. We play by the light of his reading lamp. He's ruthlessly good. He takes my queen in eleven moves.

"You're distracted," he says.

"I'm tired."

"No, you're thinking about Room 12." He moves a knight. "Everybody does, their first week. Lucy did."

My hand stops above my bishop. "Lucy?"

"The last girl. Sweet thing. Bad at chess. Worse than you." He watches me over the tops of his glasses. "She asked me a lot of questions about Marian, near the end. Right before her accident."

"What kind of questions?"

"The kind a judge knows better than to answer at two in the morning." He takes my bishop. "Check."

I stare at the board. I can't see a way out.

"Marian Hart died on a Tuesday," Mr. Pruitt says quietly. "Evelyn signed the death certificate herself. She's the facility physician, you see, so she can. The funeral home came that same afternoon. Closed casket. Buried on Thursday. I was a judge for thirty-one years, young lady. I know what a rushed verdict looks like."

"What are you saying?"

He moves his queen.

"I'm saying checkmate," Mr. Pruitt says. "Go do your rounds. It's two o'clock."

sections.title: Chapter 4
sections.html:
Chapter 4

Rule #8: There are no night visitors. If you see one, you didn't.

I sleep in a rented cabin at the bottom of the mountain, in the town of Hollis, which is one stoplight, a Dollar General, and a diner called the Blue Plate. I sleep badly. I always have after nights, even after eight years. The daylight leaks around the curtains and my body refuses to believe it's bedtime.

In the afternoon, I drive back up the mountain. Not to Hollis Ridge. Just up the road.

The seventh switchback is the sharpest. A hairpin, doubling back on itself so tightly you have to slow to fifteen. On the outside of the curve, there's a steel guardrail, and past it, the long blue drop to the valley.

There's a new section of guardrail on the curve. Shinier than the rest. And tied to one of the posts, there's a white wooden cross with a wreath of plastic flowers, faded by a summer of sun.

I pull onto the narrow shoulder and get out.

The flowers are daisies. Fake ones. There's a small laminated photo zip-tied to the center of the cross: a young woman with a round, freckled face and red hair pulled up in a messy bun, laughing at something outside the frame.

Below it, in marker, someone has written: LUCY. WE LOVE YOU.

I stand there for a long time.

A car comes down the mountain and slows beside me, a dusty Subaru with a woman inside. She rolls down her window. "You okay, hon?"

"Fine. Just stopped to look."

She glances at the cross. "Awful thing. She worked up at the Ridge. Night shift. Went through the rail at three in the morning. Car rolled all the way down to the creek." She shakes her head. "Too many people die on this road."

"Did they know what happened?"

"Said she'd been drinking." The woman shrugs. "That's what they always say."

She drives on. I crouch beside the new section of guardrail and look at the pavement. Four months of rain and sun have faded everything. But there's still a mark, if you know how to look. A long black curve of rubber, swerving hard toward the rail.

And a second mark, behind it, shorter. Straight. Like another set of tires that braked hard, and stopped.

* * *

A sheriff's cruiser pulls up behind my car. I straighten up, brushing off my knees.

The deputy who gets out is a woman about my age, with a dark braid and a tired, watchful face. Her name tag says NUNEZ.

"Afternoon," she says. "You broke down?"

"No. Just stopped."

She looks at the cross. Then at me. "You knew her?"

"I work at Hollis Ridge. I'm the new night attendant."

Something shifts in her face. "Huh. Well. Drive careful. This curve's a killer, especially in fog."

"They said she'd been drinking."

"Blood alcohol was point oh nine." Deputy Nunez says it flatly, like a fact she's stated too many times. "Over the limit. Late at night. Wet road. Sharp curve."

"Lucy didn't drink."

The words are out before I can stop them.

Deputy Nunez goes very still. She looks at me, really looks, the way I look at a monitor when a number doesn't match the patient in front of me.

"I thought you said you didn't know her," Nunez says.

"I don't. I just. Someone at work said. That she didn't drink."

The deputy studies my face. I keep it blank. I'm good at that.

"Okay," she says slowly. She takes out a card and holds it out to me. "If someone at work says anything else, you give me a call."

I take the card. My fingers are shaking. I hope she doesn't see.

She does.

sections.title: Chapter 5
sections.html:
Chapter 5

Rule #5: The east elevator is out of service. Do not get in, even if it arrives.

On my sixth night, the elevator arrives.

It's 2:40 in the morning. I'm on the east wing, finishing rounds, standing outside Mrs. Vale's door, when I hear it. A deep mechanical groan from inside the walls. The rattle of old cables. A hum.

I turn around.

At the end of the hall, the brass arrow above the elevator doors is moving. Sliding slowly along its arc. A. 3. And then it stops.

On 2.

A soft chime. And the doors open.

Behind the brass gate, the elevator car is lit. Warm yellow light spills across the hall carpet. The car is small, wood-paneled, with a brass rail and a little upholstered bench in one corner. It's empty.

The out-of-service sign is still taped to the outside of the doors. It's torn now, split down the middle where the doors parted.

I stand there with my flashlight in my hand and my heart in my throat.

Do not get in, even if it arrives.

The elevator waits. The light hums. From somewhere far above, through the open shaft, I hear something so faint I think at first I'm imagining it.

Someone is humming.

A woman's voice, thin and wavering, very old. Humming a tune I know. It takes me a second to place it. It's a song my grandmother used to sing, standing at the stove.

You are my sunshine, my only sunshine.

The doors slide shut. The arrow creeps back up its arc. 3. A.

The humming stops.

* * *

Back at the nurses' station, Tomas is asleep in his chair with his arms folded. I don't wake him. I walk into the office and sit down at the rolltop desk, and I look at the baby monitor.

It's hissing softly. Static. The row of little red lights is dark.

Then, as I watch, one light flickers.

Two.

And through the static, very faint, I hear it again. You make me happy, when skies are gray.

The same voice. The same song. Coming through the monitor.

I lean closer. My hand is reaching for the volume dial.

A thick hand closes over mine.

"Rule nine," Tomas says quietly.

He turns the volume all the way down. The red lights keep flickering, silently, dancing with the song I can no longer hear.

"Who is that?" I whisper.

Tomas looks at me for a long time. In the green light of the desk lamp, his face is all shadows.

"It's not your concern," he says. "Go do your rounds, mija. It's three o'clock."

sections.title: Chapter 6
sections.html:
Chapter 6

Rule #9: Whatever you hear on the office monitor is not your concern.

The staff locker room is in the basement, down a narrow back staircase from the kitchen. It's a dim room with a concrete floor, a humming refrigerator, and two rows of dented metal lockers, each with a strip of masking tape and a name written in marker.

Mine says CALDER. Someone wrote it in before I arrived.

The one beside it, number seven, has a strip of tape that's been peeled off, leaving a pale rectangle and a few scraps of paper. You can still read part of it. LU—

I open it. It's empty. Wiped clean. There's a faint smell of bleach, and one stubborn old coffee stain on the bottom.

I run my hand along the inside of the top shelf, the way you would if you were looking for a spare key. Nothing. I run my hand along the underside of the shelf.

Tape.

My fingernails find the edge, and I peel it back slowly, and a folded piece of paper drops into my hand.

It's a page torn from a spiral notebook, folded into a tight square. I unfold it under the flickering fluorescent light.

It's a floor plan. Hand-drawn in blue ballpoint. The second floor of Hollis Ridge: the two wings, the nurses' station, the rooms numbered one through twelve, the elevator at the end of the east hall.

But there's more. Above the west wing, above Room 12, someone has drawn a second, smaller rectangle. A room that isn't on any floor plan I've seen. And from Room 12, a dotted line runs straight up into it, with an arrow and a question mark.

12 → UP?

From the elevator, another dotted line: A = HERE.

And in the corner of the page, in small, looping handwriting, the kind that dots its i's with little circles:

She hums the sunshine song. She knows my name. She asked me to take her home.

I know that handwriting.

I know it the way you know your own face. I've seen it on birthday cards and grocery lists and angry letters. I've seen it on the back of a photograph of two little girls on a porch swing, a redhead and a brunette, with their arms around each other: Lu & Wrenny, summer '99.

I press the paper to my mouth, and I close my eyes, and for just a second I let myself shake.

"Looking for something?"

I spin around, jamming the paper into the pocket of my scrubs.

Dr. Hart stands at the bottom of the stairs. She's wearing a long camel coat and carrying a leather tote, like she's just arrived. It's 9:50 at night. She never comes in at night.

"Just putting my things away," I say. "Before my shift."

"That's Lucy's locker." Her pale eyes flick from the open door to my face. "I had it cleaned out. Her family never came for her things. Sad, really." She steps closer. "She was a troubled girl, Wren. Did you know that? She drank. She told stories. She got confused about what was real."

"I didn't know."

"No. How could you?" Dr. Hart reaches past me and closes locker seven with a soft metal click. "Rule one, Wren. Clock in at ten. It's almost time."

sections.title: Chapter 7
sections.html:
Chapter 7

Rule #6: If Mrs. Vale asks what year it is, tell her 1987.

"Why 1987?" I ask Mr. Pruitt.

It's 1 a.m. We're playing chess again. He's winning again.

"Because that's the year her husband died," he says. "Every time someone tells Adelaide the real year, she has to learn he's dead all over again. She screams for hours. So Evelyn made it a rule." He moves a pawn. "It's the one kind rule on that whole card."

"She talks about Marian. Like she's still alive. Upstairs."

"Adelaide talks about a lot of things. She thinks Reagan's president." He takes my knight. "Although."

"Although what?"

He's quiet for a long time, looking at the board. When he speaks, his voice is lower.

"Adelaide and Marian were friends for sixty years. Summers here, as girls. When Marian got sick, Adelaide moved in right after, so they could be together. They used to sit on that porch every afternoon." He looks up. "When Marian died, nobody let Adelaide see the body. Closed casket, like I said. Adelaide never believed it. She'd say, Marian's not gone, she's just upstairs. Everybody thought it was the dementia."

"And you?"

"I thought it was the dementia too." He picks up my knight and turns it over in his fingers. "Then the call light in Room 12 started going off. Every night. Around three. And Evelyn made a rule about it."

The lamp buzzes. Down the hall, somebody coughs in their sleep.

"Mr. Pruitt," I say. "Lucy asked you about Marian. What did you tell her?"

"The truth. Everything I just told you." His hands have stopped moving. "And three nights later, she went through the guardrail on the seventh switchback."

He sets my knight down on the edge of the board, very gently.

"I'm ninety-one years old, Wren. I've buried two wives and a son. I don't frighten easily. But I've been sitting in this room thinking for four months, and I'll tell you what I think. I think that girl was killed for something I said. And I think you should go home, and not come back."

"I can't."

"Why not?"

I look at the chessboard. At my king, alone in the corner, surrounded.

"Because I don't know how to leave," I say. "I never have."

sections.title: Chapter 8
sections.html:
Chapter 8

Rule #4: Never answer the call button in Room 12.

At 3:12 on my ninth night, the light above Room 12 comes on, and this time I answer it.

Tomas is on his break, down in the kitchen. I can hear him clattering around, reheating something that smells like beans and chiles. The west wing is dark and silent. The only light is that small red circle at the end of the hall, glowing above the dusty door.

I walk toward it. I don't run. Running is for emergencies, and this isn't one. It's just a call light. It's just an old building with a glitchy wire.

I have Tomas's keys. He left them on the desk when he went downstairs. The master key is the big brass one; I've watched him use it on every door in the building.

It fits Room 12.

The lock is stiff, like it hasn't been turned in a long time. I have to put my shoulder into it. And then the door swings open, and the smell hits me: dust, stale air, and underneath, faint, lilies.

I shine my flashlight around the room.

It's a resident room like all the others, but frozen. A hospital bed, made up with a white chenille spread. A nightstand with a lamp and a water pitcher. An armchair by the window with a folded afghan over one arm. Everything is coated in a soft gray film of dust. Three years of it.

On the wall beside the bed, there's the call panel. A little white box with a red button and a coiled cord.

I shine my light on it.

The dust on the button is undisturbed. Thick. Nobody's touched it in years.

But above me, on the console, the call light is still chiming.

I follow the cord from the call panel with my light. It runs up the wall to a junction box near the ceiling. And from the junction box, a second wire runs up. Newer. White plastic, not the old cloth-covered cable. It disappears through a neat hole drilled into the plaster ceiling.

Up.

12 → UP?

I step onto the armchair, dust puffing up around my shoes, and reach for the ceiling. There's a square panel up there, painted the same white as the plaster, almost invisible. An access hatch. I press on it. It doesn't budge. Locked from the other side. Or nailed.

The chiming stops.

In the sudden silence, I hear something above me. Through the ceiling. Faint and wavering and old.

Please don't take my sunshine away.

"You're not supposed to be in here."

I nearly fall off the chair.

A man is standing in the doorway. Young, maybe twenty-five, with a buzz cut and a thick neck and a black security uniform stretched over a gym body. A flashlight in one hand. The other hand rests on his belt, near a radio, near a holster.

Gus. From the gatehouse. I've seen him twice, through the window of his little booth, eating sunflower seeds and watching videos on his phone. He's never been inside the house on my shift.

"The call light went off," I say, climbing down. "I thought someone might be in here."

"Nobody's in here." Gus doesn't come in. He doesn't take his eyes off me. "Rule four. You read the card?"

"I read it."

"Then you know." He steps back to let me out. When I pass him in the doorway, he's close enough that I can smell sunflower seeds and aftershave. "Dr. Hart's gonna hear about this," he says softly. "Just so you know."

sections.title: Chapter 9
sections.html:
Chapter 9

Rule #7: The medication carts lock at two. Only Dr. Hart holds the key.

She calls me in the next evening, before my shift. Her office, not the little night office. A big room on the first floor, with a fireplace and oil paintings and a window looking out over forty miles of mountains going purple in the dusk.

"Sit," Dr. Hart says.

I sit.

She doesn't. She stands by the window with her back to me, a glass of red wine in her hand.

"Gus tells me you were in Room 12 last night."

"The call light went off. I thought—"

"You thought you'd break rule four." She turns around. Her face is calm. Her voice is calm. "Nine nights, Wren. Lucy lasted three weeks before she started breaking the rules. You made it nine nights."

I say nothing.

"I did some reading today." She sets the wineglass on the mantel. "About you. Wren Calder. Charlotte Memorial ICU, eight years, excellent evaluations. And then, in June, you took an indefinite leave of absence. Very suddenly. Your supervisor was very discreet when I called her, but she said you'd had a family emergency."

My heart is pounding so hard I can feel it in my teeth.

"Burnout," I say.

"Burnout." Dr. Hart smiles. "That's what you said at your interview. And yet here you are, working nights again, in a house full of old people who could die at any moment. That doesn't sound like someone running from burnout. That sounds like someone running toward something."

"I needed the money."

"Did you? Your credit is excellent. You own your condo." Her smile doesn't move. "I'm very thorough, Wren. I'd have to be, to run a place like this. Families trust me with the people they love most."

She walks to her desk and sits down across from me. Folds her hands.

"I'm going to give you the benefit of the doubt," she says. "Because you're a good nurse, and good nurses are hard to find at the top of a mountain. You were curious. Everyone is curious, their first few weeks. But I want to be very clear with you, the way I was clear with Lucy."

"About what?"

"About what happens to people who see things that aren't there." Her pale eyes hold mine. "Lucy started seeing things. Hearing things. She got it into her head that there was someone living in the attic. A ghost, maybe. A secret." She sighs. "She started drinking to cope. And one night she got into her car after too many, and she took the seventh switchback too fast."

"That's what the police said."

"That's what happened." Dr. Hart stands. The meeting is over. "Rule seven, Wren. The medication carts lock at two. I hold the only key. I want you to think about why I'd need to be so careful about something like that, in a house full of vulnerable people." She walks me to the door. "And I want you to think about how easy it would be for a nurse with a family emergency and a history of sudden leave to make a terrible mistake."

She opens the door for me.

"Have a quiet night," says Dr. Hart.

sections.title: Chapter 10
sections.html:
Chapter 10

Rule #4: Never answer.

I haven't told you the truth.

Not all of it. I've told you what I told Dr. Hart, and Tomas, and Mr. Pruitt, and the deputy on the seventh switchback. I've told you I'm a nurse who burned out. That part is real. The rest I've kept folded up small, the way Lucy folded that floor plan, and taped under a shelf where nobody would find it.

Here it is.

My name is Wren Calder. It used to be Wren Brandt. I kept my ex-husband's name after the divorce because I liked it better than my own, and because it made me feel like someone new.

Lucy Brandt was my little sister.

* * *

She was three years younger than me. Red hair, freckles, a laugh like a car alarm. When we were kids, she followed me everywhere. When we were teenagers, she stole my clothes. When our mother got sick, Lucy was the one who moved back home to take care of her, and I was the one who stayed in Charlotte, working doubles in the ICU, sending money and not visiting.

I told myself the money was enough. I told myself I was saving other people's mothers. I told myself a lot of things.

Mom died two and a half years ago. At the funeral, Lucy said I'd abandoned them both. I said some things back that I will never be able to take back, about her drinking, about her never finishing anything, about how easy it is to be a saint when you have nothing else going on. She threw a glass of sweet tea at me in the church fellowship hall in front of forty people.

We didn't speak for two years.

I heard from a cousin that she'd gotten sober. That she'd gotten her CNA certification. That she'd taken a job at some fancy care home up in the mountains. I thought about calling. I thought about it a hundred times. I never did.

And then, on June ninth, at 3:12 in the morning, my phone lit up on my nightstand in Charlotte.

LUCY.

I looked at it. I was half asleep. I'd worked a double. I thought, She's drunk. She's drunk and she wants to fight. I thought, Not tonight.

I turned the phone face down and went back to sleep.

At 9:40 that morning, a deputy from the county sheriff's office called to tell me my sister was dead.

* * *

I have the voicemail. Of course I do. It's still on my phone, four months later. Two minutes and fifty-one seconds long.

For four months I could only listen to the first forty seconds. Her voice, shaking. There's a woman up here who's supposed to be dead. The impact. Her scream. And then I'd stop it, every time, because I couldn't stand to hear what came after.

Tonight, in my rented cabin at the bottom of the mountain, with Lucy's floor plan spread out on the kitchen table in front of me, I put in my earbuds and listen to all of it.

The scream. The crunch of metal, the long, awful grinding of the car against the rail. A thump. Then glass, and a silence so total I think the recording has cut out.

It hasn't. After nine seconds, I hear an engine. Idling. Close.

A car door opening.

Footsteps on gravel. Slow. Careful.

Breathing, very close to the phone, as if someone is leaning in through a broken window.

And then a voice. A man. Low and calm, almost gentle, the way you'd talk to a frightened horse.

"Easy. Easy now, ——."

The last word is lost. A crackle of static, or a hand brushing the phone. One or two syllables, swallowed.

Then the footsteps go away. The door closes. The engine fades.

And the recording runs on for another minute and a half, nothing but the tick of cooling metal, and water running somewhere below, and, very faintly, a sound I finally understand is my sister breathing.

And then she stops.

* * *

I sit at the kitchen table until the sky outside turns gray.

Lucy didn't go through that guardrail because she was drunk. Somebody pushed her. Somebody stopped, and got out, and looked at her through the window, and talked to her softly, and left her there.

And that somebody works at Hollis Ridge.

I didn't take this job for the money. I didn't take it for the quiet. I took it because my sister called me for help at 3:12 in the morning, and I didn't answer.

I'm answering now.

sections.title: Chapter 11
sections.html:
Chapter 11

Rule #5: Do not get in, even if it arrives.

The elevator has a key switch.

I find it on my twelfth night, when I finally get close enough to look. Inside the car, below the row of brass buttons marked B, 1, 2, and 3, there's a small steel plate with a keyhole. No label. Just a keyhole, worn shiny around the edges from years of use.

You can't get to A without a key.

Tomas has a key he wears on a leather cord around his neck, under his scrubs. I've seen it twice: once when he bent to pick up a dropped pill cup, once when he stretched in his chair at four in the morning. A small brass key, old-fashioned, with a round head.

I've been watching Tomas the way I watch a patient whose vitals don't make sense.

He's gentle with the residents. He knows every one of them: how Mrs. Lynde likes her pillows, which songs will calm Mr. Okafor when he wakes up confused. He never raises his voice. He never hurries. But when the call light goes off above Room 12, he silences it without looking. And when the monitor in the office starts to hum, he turns it down, and sits there in the dark with his hands folded, listening to nothing.

Twenty years, Dr. Hart said. Tomas has been here twenty years.

He was here when Marian Hart was alive. He was here when she died.

He was here the night my sister went through the rail.

* * *

At four in the morning, the dead hour, I find him on the back porch, smoking a cigarette he isn't supposed to have. The fog is so thick I can barely see the railing. It beads on his gray braid like tiny pearls.

"You can have one," he says, without turning around.

"I don't smoke."

"Everybody smokes at four in the morning. Some of them just don't know it yet." He holds out the pack. I shake my head. He shrugs and puts it away.

I lean on the railing beside him. Below us, somewhere in the fog, the mountain falls away.

"Did you know Marian Hart?" I ask.

The cigarette pauses halfway to his mouth. Then continues.

"I knew her."

"What was she like?"

He's quiet for a long time. When he answers, his voice is different. Softer.

"Kind," he says. "She was kind. When I came here, twenty years ago, I was nobody. Illegal, if you want the truth. No papers, no English, nothing. The agency sent me up for one week, to fix the gutters. Marian found me eating my lunch in the truck in the rain, and she brought me inside, and she made me a sandwich, and she said, You'll stay." He smiles faintly. "I stayed. She helped me with the papers. She taught me to read English, out of her own books. She was the only one who ever called me Mr. Reyes."

"You loved her."

He doesn't deny it. He smokes.

"She sang all the time," he says. "Old songs. Silly songs." He looks at me sideways. "You've heard it. On the monitor."

My mouth goes dry. "Tomas. Is she—"

"Some doors aren't locked to keep people out, mija." He drops his cigarette and grinds it under his orthopedic shoe. "Some are locked to keep people safe."

He goes back inside. I stay on the porch in the fog with my heart slamming, and I think: He didn't say no.

And I think: Mija.

It's what he calls me. It's what he calls everyone. Mrs. Vale, Mrs. Lynde. It means my daughter, more or less. A small, soft word. Two syllables.

I don't know why it makes my skin go cold.

sections.title: Chapter 12
sections.html:
Chapter 12

Rule #8: There are no night visitors. If you see one, you didn't.

The sheriff's substation in Hollis is a cinderblock building next to the volunteer fire department. Deputy Carla Nunez meets me in a back room with a folding table and a coffee maker that smells like it hasn't been cleaned since the nineties.

"You said you didn't know her," Nunez says.

"I lied." I put my phone on the table between us. "She was my sister."

I tell her everything. The voicemail. The call at 3:12. The two years of silence. The job, the rules, the call light, the elevator, the humming on the monitor, Lucy's floor plan. I talk for twenty minutes without stopping. Nunez doesn't interrupt once. She just listens, and takes notes in a small spiral notebook, and her face gets harder and harder.

Then I hand her my earbuds and play her the voicemail.

All of it.

When it's over, she sits back in her folding chair and stares at the ceiling for a long time.

"Somebody stopped," she says finally.

"Somebody stopped."

"Our report says single-vehicle accident. No witnesses." She pulls a thick folder out of her bag. I realize she brought it with her. She'd already pulled it. "There was damage to her rear bumper. Scrape, some paint transfer, dark gray. The accident investigator figured it happened when the car rolled, hit a rock or the rail on the way down." She taps the folder. "But her car rolled front-first. I looked at the pictures again last week. After you said Lucy didn't drink."

"She'd been sober for over a year. My cousin told me. She had a chip."

"She had point oh nine in her blood."

"Then somebody put it there."

Nunez looks at me. I can see her thinking it through. Weighing it. "You understand what you're saying. You're saying someone at Hollis Ridge killed your sister. Because she saw something."

"Because she saw someone. Marian Hart."

"Marian Hart has been dead for three years. There's a death certificate. There's a grave in the Hollis Methodist cemetery. I drove past it this morning."

"Signed by her own daughter. Closed casket. Buried in two days."

Nunez rubs her eyes. "To exhume a body, I need a court order. To get a court order, I need evidence. Not a voicemail that proves somebody stopped at an accident scene. Not a humming baby monitor. Not a ninety-one-year-old judge's hunch." She leans forward. "I need to know she's alive, Wren. I need a picture. I need a face. I need something I can walk into a judge's chambers with."

"And if I get it?"

"Then I'll be up that mountain so fast it'll make your head spin." She slides a card across the table, a different one, with a cell number written on the back in pen. "But you listen to me. Your sister got close to whatever this is, and she ended up at the bottom of a ravine. If anything, anything, feels wrong up there, you get out and you call me."

I pick up the card.

"And Wren?" Nunez says. "The voice on the recording. The man. You recognize it?"

I think about the fog on the porch. The cigarette. Some doors are locked to keep people safe.

"No," I say.

It's not a lie, exactly. Not yet.

sections.title: Chapter 13
sections.html:
Chapter 13

Rule #3: If you find one in the hall, walk them back. Do not ask where they were going.

On my fourteenth night, at 2:20 a.m., I find Mrs. Vale in the west wing, standing in front of the linen closet.

"It's 1987," she tells me, before I can say anything. She looks pleased with herself. "I remembered."

"That's right, Mrs. Vale. It's very late. Let's get you back to bed."

"I can't. Marian's ringing." She points down the hall at Room 12. The call light isn't on. It's hours too early. But Mrs. Vale's face is completely certain. "She rings for me, and I go up, and we smoke on the stairs. Don't tell the nurses."

Do not ask where they were going.

"Which stairs, Mrs. Vale?"

She beams at me. And then she opens the linen closet door.

It's an ordinary closet. Shelves of white towels and folded sheets, stacks of adult briefs, a mop bucket in the corner. Mrs. Vale shuffles past all of it, to the back wall, which is covered in old beadboard painted the same cream color as the rest of the hall. She puts her small, knobby hand flat on one of the boards, near the bottom, and pushes.

It swings inward on a hidden hinge.

Behind it, there's darkness, and the cold, musty smell of old wood, and a narrow flight of stairs going up.

"The servants' stairs," Mrs. Vale whispers, delighted. "When this was a real house. The maids used them so the family wouldn't have to see them. Marian showed me when we were twelve." She giggles. "We used to hide up there and read her mother's romance novels."

My heart is going so fast it hurts.

"Mrs. Vale. Does anybody else know about these stairs?"

"Oh, no. It's a secret." She pats my cheek with a cold hand. "The red-haired girl knew. I showed her too. She was sweet. She said she'd take Marian home." Mrs. Vale's face clouds. "She didn't come back."

I swallow hard.

"I'm going to walk you to bed now," I say. "And then I'm going to come back. Okay?"

"Tell Marian I said hello." She yawns. "Tell her it's still 1987."

* * *

I put Mrs. Vale to bed. I check on Tomas: he's at the station, head bowed over a crossword. I tell him I'm going to the bathroom.

Then I go back to the linen closet, and step through the hidden door, and turn on my flashlight, and start to climb.

sections.title: Chapter 14
sections.html:
Chapter 14

Rule #9: Whatever you hear is not your concern.

The stairs are steep and narrow, barely wider than my shoulders. The treads are worn into shallow dips in the middle by a century of feet. The walls are bare plaster, cracked and stained, and there are cobwebs in every corner. But on the stairs themselves, there's no dust.

Somebody uses these stairs.

I count them as I go. Twenty-two. At the top there's a small landing and a plain wooden door with an old-fashioned latch.

Through the door, I can hear her humming.

You are my sunshine, my only sunshine.

I lift the latch.

* * *

It's not an attic.

It's a bedroom. A beautiful one. Low slanted ceilings painted soft blue, with little dormer windows curtained in white lace. A braided rug on the floor. A rocking chair. Shelves of old books with cracked leather spines. A dresser covered in framed photographs. A vase of fresh lilies on the windowsill.

And a hospital bed, the good kind, with an air mattress and padded rails. Beside it, an IV pole. A feeding pump. A monitor clipped to the rail, the other half of the baby monitor in the office downstairs. A call button on a long cord, the same model as the one in Room 12, with the white wire running from its box down through the floor.

In the bed, there's a woman.

She's so small. That's my first thought. So small, like a bird, a tiny shape under a quilt, with a halo of thin white hair on the pillow. Her face is a map of wrinkles, her skin almost translucent. Her hands, resting on top of the quilt, are all bones and blue veins.

She's the most beautiful thing I have ever seen, because she's alive.

"Marian?" I whisper.

The old woman stops humming. She turns her head on the pillow, slowly, and looks at me with cloudy, pale gray eyes. Evelyn's eyes.

"Are you the new girl?" she says. Her voice is thin as paper.

"Yes. I'm. My name is Wren."

"The last girl promised she'd come back." Marian's hand moves on the quilt, reaching. "She said she'd take me home. She had red hair."

I take her hand. It's cold and light, like holding a handful of twigs.

"She wanted to come back," I say. My voice breaks. "She tried. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry."

"This is my home," Marian says, and her eyes wander toward the window, toward the black night outside. "But Evie says it's not safe. Evie says the bad men will take the house if they know I'm here." She frowns. "What year is it?"

I think of Mrs. Vale. Of the kindest rule on the card.

"It's 1987," I tell her.

Marian smiles.

* * *

I take out my phone. My hands are shaking so badly I have to try three times. I photograph her: her face on the pillow, the IV, the feeding pump. I photograph the dresser, the framed photos, and when I look closer I see that one of them is a wedding picture, a young couple on the front steps of Hollis Ridge, and the bride has Marian's cheekbones. I photograph a pill organizer on the nightstand, labeled in neat block letters: M.H. I photograph a newspaper on the rocking chair. Yesterday's date.

Then I hear it. Through the floor. A deep mechanical groan. The rattle of cables. A hum.

The elevator.

It's coming up.

On the far side of the room, there's a door I didn't notice. Plain, painted blue like the walls. Beside it, a small brass plate with a single letter.

A.

I let go of Marian's hand and run for the servants' door. I get through it, and pull it almost closed, just as I hear the elevator gate rattle open on the other side of the room.

Through the crack, I watch Dr. Evelyn Hart walk into her mother's bedroom.

She's in a silk bathrobe, her silver hair loose around her shoulders. She looks younger like this. Softer. She goes straight to the bed and sits on the edge of it and takes her mother's hand, and she says, "Hi, Mama," in a voice I would never have believed could come out of her.

"Evie." Marian smiles. "The new girl was here."

Dr. Hart goes very still.

"Was she, Mama?"

"She has a bird name. She held my hand."

Dr. Hart doesn't move for a long moment. Then she pats her mother's hand, and stands up, and takes a cell phone out of the pocket of her robe.

"Gus," she says quietly, with her back to the bed. "The new one's been upstairs. I want to know who she really is. Everything. Tonight."

A pause.

"No," Dr. Hart says. "Not like the last one. Not yet."

sections.title: Chapter 15
sections.html:
Chapter 15

Rule #1: Never stay late.

I clock out at six on the dot. I say good morning to the day nurse. I walk to my car like it's any other morning, and I drive down the eleven switchbacks at exactly the speed limit, and I don't look in my rearview mirror, because I'm afraid of what I'll see.

Nothing follows me.

At the Blue Plate Diner, I sit in a back booth and send the photos to Deputy Nunez. All of them. Then I text: She's alive. She's in a hidden room above Room 12. Hart knows I found her.

Nunez calls me four minutes later.

"Jesus, Wren." I can hear her breathing, hear a car door slam. "Okay. Okay. Listen. An old woman in a bed isn't enough on its own. Hart's lawyer will say it's another resident, some private-pay patient in a special suite. I need to confirm it's Marian Hart."

"The photos. The wedding picture. The pill organizer. M.H."

"I know. It helps. It's a start." She's quiet for a second. "Here's what I can do. There's a thing called a welfare check. If I have reasonable concern that a vulnerable adult is in danger, I can go in and look. No warrant. But I have to do it right, or Hart's lawyer will get anything I find thrown out."

"When?"

"I need to talk to the county attorney first. Today. Maybe tomorrow night." She hesitates. "Can you hold on that long?"

I think about Dr. Hart on the phone. Not like the last one. Not yet.

"Yes," I say.

* * *

When I get back to my cabin, the door is open.

Not broken. Open. Standing a few inches ajar, the way you'd leave it if you'd stepped out for just a second.

I stand on the gravel with my car keys clenched between my fingers like a weapon. After a long minute, I push the door the rest of the way open with my foot.

Nothing is broken. Nothing is torn apart. The cabin looks almost exactly the way I left it. Almost.

The cardboard box I kept under the bed is gone.

Lucy's box. Everything the county sent me after she died. Her wallet. Her keys. Her sobriety chip, one year, bronze. The photograph of two little girls on a porch swing. Lu & Wrenny, summer '99.

On the kitchen table, where Lucy's floor plan was spread out when I left, there's nothing. The floor plan is gone too.

In its place, there's a single laminated card.

HOLLIS RIDGE: NIGHT SHIFT RULES.

Someone has circled rule number one in red marker.

Clock in at ten. Clock out at six. Never stay late.

And my phone buzzes in my hand. A text. A number I don't know.

Get some sleep, Ms. Brandt. You have a shift tonight.

sections.title: Chapter 16
sections.html:
Chapter 16

Rule #7: Only Dr. Hart holds the key.

I go.

Of course I go. If I don't clock in at ten, she'll know I'm running, and she'll move Marian before Nunez can get a welfare check. Or worse. I think of the dozens of bottles in those locked medication carts. I think about how very, very easy it is to make an old woman's heart stop.

So I drive up the mountain at 9:40, through fog so thick my headlights just bounce back at me, and I park in my usual spot, and I walk inside.

Dr. Hart is waiting at the nurses' station.

She's dressed for work again. Navy dress, pearls, silver hair in a neat twist. She smiles when she sees me. On the desk in front of her, there's a photograph. I recognize it from across the hall.

Two little girls on a porch swing.

"Wren Brandt," Dr. Hart says pleasantly. "Please. Sit."

Tomas isn't here. The station is empty. Down both wings, the doors are closed and dark.

I don't sit.

"Where's Tomas?"

"I gave him the night off. I thought we should talk, just the two of us." She slides the photograph across the desk toward me. "She looks like you. Around the eyes. I don't know how I missed it."

"You killed her."

"No." Dr. Hart says it simply, without heat. "I didn't. I want you to hear me say that, because it's true. I've never killed anyone in my life."

"Then who did?"

She doesn't answer. Instead she sits back in the chair and folds her hands and looks at me with those pale gray eyes. And I see, suddenly, how very tired she is.

"My mother was diagnosed with Alzheimer's six years ago," she says. "Hollis Ridge was already failing. The family money ran out a generation ago. I turned the house into this"—she gestures at the halls—"to keep it. To keep her in it. It was the only home she ever loved. But places like this are expensive, Wren. The insurance, the staffing, the lawsuits. By three years ago, we were eight months from bankruptcy. The bank was going to take the house. Sell it to some developer who'd turn it into condos. And my mother would have gone to a state facility in Asheville, in a room with three other women, and she would have died there, alone and terrified, not knowing where she was."

"So you faked her death."

"My mother had a life insurance policy. Three million dollars. My father bought it in 1987, the year before he died." A thin smile. "I'm the facility physician. I sign the death certificates. The funeral director owed me a favor. And the casket was very, very heavy."

"And you hid her in the attic."

"I moved her upstairs. To the room she grew up in. Where she could look out at the mountains. Where I could see her every night." Her voice cracks, just slightly. "She doesn't know. She thinks it's 1987 half the time. She's happy, Wren. She's safe. She's home. And Hollis Ridge is solvent, and eleven other families have a beautiful place for the people they love. Who, exactly, did I hurt?"

"Lucy," I say.

The name lands between us like a stone.

Dr. Hart looks away.

"Lucy was an accident," she says quietly.

"Lucy was sober. Lucy was run off the road. I have a recording, Dr. Hart. I have the whole thing. I have someone stopping. Getting out. Talking to her. And leaving her there to die."

For the first time since I met her, Evelyn Hart looks afraid.

Her eyes flick past me. Down the east wing. Toward the gatehouse, far out there in the fog, where a young man in a black uniform sits eating sunflower seeds.

It's less than a second. But I see it.

"Go home, Wren," she says, very softly. "I'll pay you whatever you want. A year's salary. Two. Just go home and forget this place, and let my mother die in her own bed."

"No."

She closes her eyes.

"Then I can't help you," she says. "I'm so sorry. I really did try."

sections.title: Chapter 17
sections.html:
Chapter 17

Rule #2: Every door. Every resident.

Tomas finds me at five in the morning, sitting on the back porch in the fog, shaking.

He wasn't gone. He never left. He was in his truck in the staff lot, he tells me, sleeping, because he didn't trust whatever Dr. Hart had planned. He sits down beside me on the top step without a word, and after a while, he puts his big, rough hand on my back, between my shoulder blades, and leaves it there.

"She knows," I say. "She knows who I am. She knows I found Marian."

"I know."

"Tomas. I need you to tell me the truth."

He doesn't take his hand away.

"I bring Marian her breakfast," he says. "Every morning, before I go home. I change her sheets. I brush her hair. I sing to her when she's scared." His voice is rough. "Three years. I told myself it was kindness. That Evelyn was doing a good thing, a loving thing, keeping her mother home. That the lie didn't hurt nobody."

"It hurt my sister."

"Yes." He bows his head. "Your sister. She found the stairs. She found Marian. She was going to call someone, the state, the police. Take Marian away to some hospital where she'd die with strangers." He's quiet for a long moment. "Evelyn was so frightened. And Gus."

"Gus?"

"Evelyn's nephew. Her sister's boy. She gave him a job when nobody else would. He'd do anything for her." Tomas's hand tightens on my back. "The night your sister died, Gus left the gatehouse at three in the morning. I saw his taillights go down the mountain. He came back forty minutes later. He didn't talk to nobody for a week."

My whole body has gone cold. "Why didn't you tell the police?"

"Tell them what? That a man drove down a mountain?" He shakes his head. "And they would ask why. And then they would find Marian."

"Tomas. Deputy Nunez is coming. A welfare check. Tomorrow night, maybe. She's going to come and look for Marian, and she's going to find her, and all of this is going to come out. All of it."

He's quiet for a long time. The fog swirls around us. Somewhere in the trees, a bird starts to sing, even though it's still dark.

"Good," Tomas says finally.

I look at him.

"She deserves to be found," he says. "Not hidden. Not a secret. Marian Hart. She should get to be a person again, even if it's only for a little while." He takes his hand from my back and reaches under the collar of his scrubs and pulls out the leather cord. The small brass key swings from it, glinting in the porch light. "When your deputy comes, you tell me. I'll take her up myself."

He lifts the cord over his head and presses the key into my palm and closes my fingers over it.

"In case," he says. "In case something happens to me."

I look down at the key. It's warm from his skin.

"Thank you," I whisper.

"Don't thank me, mija." Tomas stands up, his knees cracking. "Go home. Sleep. You're going to need it."

sections.title: Chapter 18
sections.html:
Chapter 18

Rule #7: The medication carts lock at two. Only Dr. Hart holds the key.

Nunez texts me at 4:15 in the afternoon.

County attorney signed off. Welfare check tonight. I'll be there at 3 a.m. with a deputy from Asheville and an adult protective services worker. Don't do anything until you see my lights.

I read it six times. Then I lie on my bed in the cabin and stare at the ceiling until it's time to go.

* * *

When I get to the nurses' station at ten, Dr. Hart is waiting for me again.

She doesn't mention last night. She doesn't mention Lucy, or Marian, or the photograph of two girls on a porch swing. She's wearing her camel coat and holding her car keys, and she looks the way she did the day I met her: composed, polished, perfectly in control.

"I have to go to Asheville tonight," she says. "A family matter. I'll be back in the morning."

"Okay."

She holds out a small silver key on a red plastic tag.

"The medication carts," she says. "I'll be out of reach. If someone needs something after two, you're the most qualified person in this building." A thin smile. "Consider it a gesture of trust."

I look at the key in her palm. Rule seven. Only Dr. Hart holds the key. In three weeks, I've never seen her hand it to anyone. Not the day nurses. Not Tomas.

"I don't want it," I say.

"It's not optional, Wren. It's the job." She sets it on the desk in front of me. "Every door. Every resident."

She walks away down the stairs. I hear the front door close, and a car start, and tires crunch away across the gravel. I go to the window at the end of the east wing and watch her taillights snake down the mountain, one switchback, two, three, until the fog swallows them.

When I turn around, Tomas is standing at the station, looking at the key on the desk.

"She gave you that?" he says.

"She said it was a gesture of trust."

Tomas picks it up by the red tag, like it's something dead, and puts it in the drawer, and closes the drawer.

"Don't touch it again," he says. "Not for nobody."

* * *

The gatehouse is dark.

I notice it at eleven, on my first round, when I look out the window at the bottom of the west wing. Every night for three weeks, there's been a light in that little booth at the end of the drive, and the blue glow of Gus's phone. Tonight there's nothing. Just fog and the black shape of the booth.

"Where's Gus?" I ask Tomas.

He looks out the window for a long time.

"I don't know," he says.

sections.title: Chapter 19
sections.html:
Chapter 19

Rule #2: Rounds every hour, on the hour.

At 1:50 a.m., Mr. Pruitt stops breathing.

I find him on my two o'clock round. I'm ten minutes early, because I can't sit still, because I keep looking at the clock and doing math. Seventy minutes until Nunez. Sixty-nine. I push open his door, and his reading lamp is on, and the chessboard is set up by the window, and he's in bed with his eyes half closed.

His chest isn't moving.

Eight years in the ICU. My body moves before my mind does. I'm across the room. I've got two fingers on his carotid. There's a pulse, faint and slow. His lips are gray. I thumb open one eyelid. The pupil is a pinpoint, a tiny black dot, like the head of a pin.

Opioids.

Mr. Pruitt doesn't take opioids. I've read his chart. Blood pressure pills and a stool softener and eye drops. He's a ninety-one-year-old man with a mind like a steel trap and a body held together with string, and somebody has filled him with enough narcotic to stop his heart.

"Tomas!" I scream. "Room 1! Bring the crash bag!"

I tilt his head back. I give him two rescue breaths. His chest rises. I grab my own bag off my shoulder, the black canvas bag I carry every shift, have carried every shift for eight years, and I dig through it until my fingers close on a small plastic box.

Naloxone. Nasal spray. I've carried it since the day I found out my sister was an addict. I never took it out, even after she got sober. Even after she died.

I spray it into his nose. I breathe for him. I count. One, two, three.

"Come on, Judge. Come on. Don't you dare."

Thirty seconds. Forty.

Mr. Pruitt gasps.

It's a terrible sound, a huge, rasping, desperate intake of air, and his whole body jerks, and his eyes fly open, wide and wild. He coughs. He grabs my wrist with a hand like a claw.

"There you are," I say, and I'm crying. "There you are. You're okay. You're okay."

Tomas is in the doorway with the crash bag, breathing hard.

"Call 911," I tell him. "Tell them opioid overdose, responsive after naloxone, he'll need transport."

Tomas stares at Mr. Pruitt. At me. Then he turns and runs for the phone.

* * *

Mr. Pruitt's lips are moving. I lean close.

"Visitor," he whispers. His voice is a rasp. "Night visitor."

"Who?"

"Big man. Black clothes." He coughs. "Gave me a glass of water. Said Dr. Hart sent it. To help me sleep." His grip on my wrist tightens. "Rule eight, Wren. There are no night visitors."

* * *

When Tomas comes back, I leave him with Mr. Pruitt and run to the nurses' station.

The medication cart is sitting in its usual spot. Locked, the little light on the keypad red. I pull open the desk drawer where Tomas put Dr. Hart's key.

It's gone.

I stare at the empty drawer. Then I look at the cart's little digital display. It keeps a log. Every time it's opened, it records the time and the key that opened it.

01:22. KEY 07. HYDROMORPHONE 8MG x4.

Key 07. The red plastic tag. The key Dr. Hart handed me with a smile and a gesture of trust.

Four tablets of hydromorphone, missing, signed out on my key, twenty-eight minutes before I found a ninety-one-year-old man with pinpoint pupils.

And an ICU nurse on sudden leave, with a family emergency and a dead sister who drank.

I understand now. I understand all of it.

I was never supposed to find Mr. Pruitt in time. I was supposed to find him at two o'clock, like the rules say. Dead. And in the morning, when the police came, they'd find the log, and the key, and me.

sections.title: Chapter 20
sections.html:
Chapter 20

Rule #5: Do not get in, even if it arrives.

I call Nunez. It rings five times before she picks up. There's wind on the line, and a strange echo, like she's outside.

"Wren. I'm on the mountain. We've got a problem."

"Someone tried to kill Mr. Pruitt. Opioids. I brought him back. He said a man in black came into his room. Gus. It has to be Gus. And they set it up so it looks like me."

A long, sharp breath. "Okay. Listen to me. There's a car across the road at the seventh switchback. Black Dodge Charger, parked sideways, blocking both lanes. Nobody in it. Keys gone. We can't get around it, there's no shoulder." I hear her running now, footsteps on asphalt. "We're coming on foot. It's two miles. Twenty minutes, maybe twenty-five. Get somewhere safe and lock the door."

"Marian—"

"Wren. Somewhere safe."

The line goes dead.

I stand at the station with the phone in my hand. Down the west wing, I can hear Tomas murmuring to Mr. Pruitt, low and soothing, in Spanish. The ambulance can't get up the mountain either. Nobody can get up the mountain. Somebody made sure of that.

Not like the last one. Not yet.

Tonight is yet.

I think of Marian in her little blue room at the top of the house. Her bird bones. Her hand in mine. The last girl promised she'd come back.

I run.

* * *

The linen closet. The back wall. I push on the board, near the bottom, the way Mrs. Vale showed me.

It doesn't move.

I push harder. I throw my shoulder against it. I get down and look and see the bright silver heads of new screws, four of them, driven through the edge of the board into the frame. Fresh sawdust on the floor. Someone sealed it. Today.

There's only one other way up.

At the end of the east wing, the elevator waits behind its brass gate. The torn out-of-service sign hangs in two limp halves. The arrow on the dial points to 2.

It's already here. Like it's been waiting for me.

I pull the gate open. Step inside. The car is warm and yellow and smells like old wood and lilies. I dig under my scrubs for the leather cord Tomas gave me, the small brass key, and fit it into the keyhole below the buttons.

I turn it.

The doors slide shut. The car shudders, groans, and starts to rise.

3.

The arrow creeps along its arc.

And then, between 3 and A, the elevator stops.

The lights go out.

sections.title: Chapter 21
sections.html:
Chapter 21

Rule #9: Not your concern.

Darkness. Total. The kind that presses on your eyes.

I stand very still in the dead elevator with my heart slamming against my ribs. I can hear my own breath, loud and ragged. I can hear the cables creak above me. I can hear, very faintly, through the walls of the shaft, the sound of an old woman humming.

You'll never know, dear, how much I love you.

I get my phone out. No signal. Of course. I turn on the flashlight and point it at the ceiling. There's a square hatch in the wood paneling, with a simple sliding latch. Emergency exit.

I climb onto the little upholstered bench and stretch as far as I can, and my fingers find the latch, and it slides, and the hatch lifts. Cold, dusty air pours down on me. Above, in the flashlight beam, there's the black throat of the shaft, a greasy tangle of cables, and on one wall, a narrow steel ladder bolted into the brick.

Four feet above the top of the car, there's a pair of closed doors. With a brass plate beside them.

A.

I haul myself up through the hatch. I've never been strong. But I've lifted three-hundred-pound men off the floor during codes, and I've done chest compressions for forty minutes straight, and it turns out that when you have to, your body remembers every single thing it's ever done.

I climb the ladder. I wedge my fingers between the elevator doors. And I pull.

* * *

They slide apart on the blue bedroom.

The lamp on the dresser is on. The lilies on the windowsill glow white. Marian Hart is lying in her bed, humming, her eyes half closed.

And sitting on the edge of the bed, holding a syringe, is her daughter.

Evelyn Hart never went to Asheville. She's still in her camel coat. Her silver hair has come loose from its twist, and her face is wet with tears, and she's holding the syringe in both hands in her lap, like a prayer book. It's full. Twenty milliliters, clear liquid.

She looks up at me without surprise.

"Of course," she says. "Of course it's you."

"Evelyn." I step out of the elevator shaft into the room, very slowly. I keep my hands where she can see them. "What's in the syringe?"

"Morphine." She says it simply. "A lot of it. It won't hurt. She'll just go to sleep." She looks down at her mother. "She died three years ago, Wren. Everyone knows that. There's a stone in the cemetery with her name on it. I'm only making it true."

"You don't have to do this."

"There are police on the mountain. I heard them on Gus's radio." She laughs, a small, broken sound. "In an hour this room will be full of strangers. They'll put her in an ambulance. They'll take her to some hospital in Asheville, and she'll wake up with strangers, not knowing where she is, and she'll be terrified. And she'll die there. Alone." Her hands tighten on the syringe. "I promised her. I promised her she'd die at home."

"Evelyn. Look at me."

She does. Her pale eyes are swimming.

"I'm a nurse," I say. "I've been with hundreds of people when they die. I've held their hands. I've held their families' hands. I know what a good death looks like, and I know what a bad one looks like. This"—I nod at the syringe—"this isn't for her. This is for you. So you don't have to face what you did."

"What I did—"

"Mr. Pruitt is alive," I say. "I found him in time. Somebody gave him four hydromorphone and signed them out on the key you gave me. Did you know that? Did you know what Gus was going to do?"

Her face goes white.

"No," Evelyn whispers. "No. I told him to watch you. I told him to keep you away from her. I never told him to—"

"Evie."

We both freeze.

Marian's eyes are open. Clear. Clearer than I've ever seen them, gray and steady. She's looking at her daughter. And one small, skeletal hand is lifting from the quilt, reaching toward the syringe.

"Evie," Marian says again, in a voice that's suddenly a mother's voice, firm and quiet and certain. "Stop that. Put it down."

Evelyn Hart's face crumples like paper.

The syringe slips out of her fingers and rolls across the braided rug, and she folds over onto the bed and puts her head on her mother's chest, and she sobs. Big, ugly, child's sobs. And Marian Hart, who thinks it's 1987, strokes her daughter's silver hair with one bony hand, over and over.

"There, there," she murmurs. "There, there, my sunshine."

I pick up the syringe. I'm reaching for my phone to call Nunez when I hear the door to the servants' stairs slam open behind me.

"Nobody move," says Gus.

sections.title: Chapter 22
sections.html:
Chapter 22

Rule #8: If you see one, you didn't.

He's holding a pistol. Black, square, ugly. He's pointing it at me.

He's breathing hard, and his black uniform is wet with fog, and there's a screwdriver sticking out of his back pocket. He came up the servants' stairs. He's the one who sealed them, and then he came up them anyway, unscrewing the board from inside. Of course he did. He's been ahead of me the whole time.

"Aunt Evie," Gus says, not taking his eyes off me. "Get away from her."

"Gus." Evelyn lifts her head from the bed. Her face is swollen, streaked with mascara. "Gus, what did you do? Mr. Pruitt—"

"The old man was gonna talk. He'd been talking to her." Gus jerks the gun at me. "You said handle it. You said you couldn't lose this place. You said you couldn't lose Grandma."

"I never said—"

"You said handle it!" His voice cracks, high and young. "Like the last one! You said handle it about the last one, too, and I tried, and you never said thank you, you never said anything, you just gave me a raise and never looked at me again—"

"Gus." I keep my voice very calm. "Put the gun down. The police are coming up the road right now. It's over."

"It's not over." He's sweating now, I can see it on his upper lip. "It's not over till I say. Here's what happened. The crazy nurse OD'd the judge. And then she came up here to hurt Grandma. And I stopped her." His finger moves on the trigger. "That's what happened."

"Gus, no," Evelyn says.

"Close your eyes, Aunt Evie."

And behind him, in the dark of the servants' stairwell, something moves.

It's Tomas.

He comes up those last steps like a bull, low and fast and silent, and he hits Gus from behind with his whole thick body, and they go down together in a tangle of arms and legs. The gun goes off. The sound is huge in that small room. The lamp on the dresser explodes in a shower of glass, and the room goes half dark, lit only by the moon through the lace curtains.

Gus is screaming. Tomas is on top of him, one knee in his back, both hands pinning Gus's wrist to the floor, the gun just out of reach. I kick it across the rug, under the bed.

"Wren," Tomas grunts. "The syringe. Throw it out the window."

I look down at my hand. I'm still holding it. Twenty milliliters of morphine.

I don't throw it. I hold it very carefully, cap on, in my closed fist, pressed against my chest.

Because it's evidence.

And then there are lights. Red and blue, strobing across the fog outside the dormer windows. Voices on the stairs. Deputy Carla Nunez comes through the servants' door with her gun drawn and her braid half undone, gasping like she's run two miles uphill, because she has.

She takes in the room. Gus on the floor, Tomas on top of him. Evelyn Hart on the bed, weeping. Me, holding a syringe.

And in the bed, an old woman with white hair and pale gray eyes, looking at all these strangers with polite, puzzled interest.

"Oh, hello," Marian Hart says to the deputy. "Are you here for the party? What year is it?"

sections.title: Chapter 23
sections.html:
Chapter 23

Rule #1: Never stay late.

I stay late.

I stay until the sun comes up over the Blue Ridge, turning the fog pink and gold. I stay while the paramedics carry Mr. Pruitt down the front steps on a stretcher. He's grumbling that he wants his chessboard, and he's alive, and he gives me a thumbs-up as they load him into the ambulance. I stay while two deputies walk Gus out in handcuffs, his face gray, his uniform torn. I stay while Evelyn Hart sits on the front porch in one of the white rocking chairs, with a female deputy beside her, not speaking, staring out at the mountains she did all of this to keep.

I stay while Adult Protective Services takes Marian away.

They're gentle with her. I'll give them that. The social worker is a kind, heavyset woman named Denise who speaks softly and calls her Mrs. Hart, and they let Tomas ride with her in the ambulance, holding her hand. Before they close the doors, Marian looks back at the house over Tomas's shoulder.

"Tell Adelaide I'll see her tomorrow," she says.

"I'll tell her," I say.

* * *

It takes weeks for all of it to come out. It comes out anyway. That's the thing about secrets. You can nail them into the walls, you can bury them in heavy caskets, you can hide them in blue rooms at the tops of houses. They come out.

Gus is charged with attempted murder for Mr. Pruitt, and aggravated assault, and a dozen other things. His Charger is towed off the seventh switchback. It's black, not dark gray. His lawyer makes a point of that.

Evelyn Hart is charged with insurance fraud, falsifying a death certificate, abuse of a vulnerable adult, and obstruction. She hires the most expensive lawyer in North Carolina, and then, a week later, she fires him and pleads guilty to everything. The papers say she wept in court. The papers say she asked the judge only one thing: that her mother be allowed to stay at Hollis Ridge.

The judge said no. Hollis Ridge is closed now. The residents have gone to other homes. The bank has the house.

Mrs. Vale went to a memory care place in Asheville, the same one they moved Marian to. They share a room. I've visited twice. Both times, they were sitting side by side in two recliners by the window, holding hands, watching birds at the feeder. Both times, Mrs. Vale asked me what year it was.

Both times, I said 1987.

* * *

The part I care about, the only part, takes longer.

In a recorded interview with Deputy Nunez, Gus confesses to a lot of things. He confesses to drugging Mr. Pruitt. He confesses to sealing the servants' stairs, to parking his car across the road, to breaking into my cabin and stealing Lucy's box, which they find in the trunk of his Charger, every single thing still inside.

He confesses that on the night of June ninth, his aunt called him at 2:50 in the morning and told him Lucy had been upstairs, had seen Marian, was leaving, and that he needed to handle it.

He confesses that he followed Lucy's car down the mountain.

But he swears, over and over, crying, that he never touched her.

"I was scared," he tells Nunez on the recording. I've listened to it. She played it for me. "I was just gonna follow her. Scare her. Make her pull over so I could talk to her. But she was way ahead of me. And when I came around the seventh curve, she was already gone. The rail was already busted. Her car was already at the bottom. I could see the headlights down there in the creek. And I panicked, and I turned around and went back up, and I never told nobody."

"Then who ran her off the road?" Nunez asks.

"I don't know." Gus's voice breaks. "I swear to God. I don't know."

Nobody believes him. Not Nunez, not the district attorney, not the jury, I'm sure, when it gets to trial.

I want to believe he's lying. I want it more than I've ever wanted anything.

But I've listened to my sister's voicemail again. Every night, now. All two minutes and fifty-one seconds. And the man's voice on the recording, the voice that says Easy, easy now, the voice that leans into her broken window and talks to her like a frightened horse—

It's not Gus.

Gus is twenty-five. Gus's voice is thin and high and cracks when he's scared.

The voice on my sister's voicemail is older. Deep. Calm.

Almost gentle.

sections.title: Epilogue
sections.html:
Epilogue

Rule #4: Never answer the call button in Room 12.

Marian Hart dies on a Sunday in December, in her sleep, with the winter sun coming through the window and Adelaide Vale holding her hand.

They bury her in the Hollis Methodist cemetery. The old grave is still there, the one with her name and a date three years wrong. They dig it up and take out the heavy casket full of sandbags, and then they put Marian in, the real Marian, and they fill it in again. It's a small service. Mr. Pruitt comes in a wheelchair and grumbles through the whole thing. Mrs. Vale sings "You Are My Sunshine" in a high, cracked voice, and everyone cries.

Tomas stands at the back, in a black suit that's too tight across the shoulders, holding his hat. He doesn't sing. He doesn't cry. He just stands there, and when it's over, he's the first to leave.

I follow him.

* * *

He lives in a small white house at the end of a dirt road, about five miles out of town, with a garden gone to seed and a porch full of wind chimes. I've never been here before. I found the address in the Hollis Ridge staff files, the day before they closed the building for good. Before I get out of my car, I text it to Deputy Nunez, along with four words: Come. Park out of sight.

His truck is in the carport. An old Ford pickup.

It's green.

It's been green, I think, for a few months. The paint is too fresh, too glossy. Somebody did a careful job, but not a professional one. There's a drip of paint on the side mirror. There's tape residue along the edge of the windshield.

And on the front bumper, down low, on the right side, where the new green paint has chipped away against a curb or a rock, the old color shows through.

Dark gray.
