I stand in the carport and look at that little chip of gray paint for a long time.

Every night for three weeks, Tomas's truck sat in the staff lot at Hollis Ridge. I parked right next to it. I never looked at it. Why would I? It was just an old green truck.

"You figured it out."

Tomas is on the porch. He's taken off his suit jacket. He's holding his hat in both hands, turning it slowly by the brim.

"She was going to take Marian away," he says quietly. "Your sister. She told me, that night, before she left. She said, Mr. Reyes, I'm calling the state in the morning. They'll put her somewhere safe." His hands tighten on the hat. "But Marian was already safe. She was home. And I thought, if they take her, she will die in a room full of strangers, not knowing anybody. Not knowing me."

"So you followed her."

"I only wanted to talk to her. I flashed my lights. She wouldn't stop. She went faster." He closes his eyes. "I pushed a little. Just a little. Just to make her stop. And the road was wet."

My whole body is shaking.

"You stopped," I say. "After. You got out. I heard you. On the recording."

He opens his eyes. He looks surprised, and then he looks very, very tired.

"She was still alive," Tomas says. "Hurt bad. Her head. I talked to her. I held her hand through the window. I told her it was okay. I had a flask in the truck. Whiskey. I made her drink some, for the pain." He swallows. "And then I poured the rest over her. On her shirt. In the car. So they would say what they always say."

"You left her there."

"I couldn't save her, mija. Nobody could have saved her." His voice cracks. "And if I called, they would ask why I was on the road. And they would find Marian."

Easy. Easy now, mija.

Two syllables. Swallowed by static. I've listened to them a thousand times.

I know what they are now.

* * *

I don't say anything else. There's nothing else to say. I walk back to my car, and I get in, and I start the engine, and Tomas doesn't try to stop me. He just stands on his porch among the wind chimes with his hat in his hands, watching me go.

At the end of his dirt road, I pull over.

My phone is in my coat pocket. It's been there the whole time, recording. I started it in the carport, when I saw the gray paint under the green. I learned that from Lucy. The last thing she ever taught me.

I stop the recording. I save it.

Then my phone buzzes in my hand.

A call. Unknown number. The Hollis area code.

For a second I think it's Tomas, calling to beg, or explain, or tell me one more time that he loved her. For a second I think of rule four, laminated on a card in a closed-down house at the top of a mountain. Never answer.

I think of June ninth. 3:12 in the morning. A phone lighting up on a nightstand in Charlotte. A name on the screen. A woman turning over and going back to sleep.

This time, I answer.

"Wren?" It's Deputy Nunez. "I got your text. I'm at the end of the road. I can see your car." A pause. "Are you okay?"

I look in my rearview mirror at the little white house, and the wind chimes, and the old man on the porch.

"I have something for you," I tell her. "I know who stopped."

sections.title: Author’s Note
sections.html:
Author’s Note

Thank you for reading The Night Shift Rules.

If you read Rule Number Nine, you already know I have a weakness for lists of rules and the people who break them. This time I wanted to turn that idea around. What if the heroine wasn’t stumbling into a mystery, but walking straight toward one on purpose, hiding her real reason from everyone, including you?

Wren is braver than Nora in some ways and more stubborn in others. What they share is a phone call they didn’t answer, or a moment they didn’t act, and a chance to make it right. I think a lot of us carry one of those.

Hollis Ridge, the town of Hollis, and the seventh switchback are invented, though the Blue Ridge fog is very real, and it really does roll across those mountain roads like a slow white river.

If this story kept you up past your own night shift, I’d be grateful if you left a review on Amazon. Reviews are how independent books find their readers, and I read every one.

And the next time a phone rings at three in the morning, answer it.

— Sunday Pastores
